---
title: "Your First App"
description: "A complete host and phone client on one port: expose an action, emit an event, pair by QR, and install to the home screen."
---

The [Quickstart](/quickstart) proves the connection works with two Node
processes. This page builds the thing you would actually ship: a host that
**serves its own client page**, so the phone loads a URL, scans nothing twice,
and can install the result to its home screen.

## 1. Project

```bash
mkdir lamp && cd lamp && npm init -y
npm install @crosslink/sdk-node
npm install --save-dev esbuild @crosslink/sdk-browser
```

The browser SDK is a dev dependency because it gets bundled into the page the
host serves, rather than imported at runtime by Node.

## 2. Capabilities first

Decide what a paired phone may do before writing a handler. Every capability is
a promise to the user in the pairing prompt, so name them for what they let
someone do, not for the function they call.

```js
const capabilities = [
  { id: "lamp.read",  title: "See whether the lamp is on", risk: "low"  },
  { id: "lamp.write", title: "Turn the lamp on and off",   risk: "medium" }
];
```

`risk` drives the default policy: `low` may be auto-granted, `medium` and above
require a human decision. See [Capabilities and RPC](/build/capabilities-and-rpc).

## 3. The host

`host.mjs`:

```js
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { createCrosslinkServer } from "@crosslink/sdk-node";

let on = false;

const server = createCrosslinkServer({
  application: {
    id: "com.example.lamp",
    name: "Lamp",
    version: "1.0.0",
    pwaConfig: { shortName: "Lamp", themeColor: "#0f172a", startUrl: "/" }
  },
  capabilities: [
    { id: "lamp.read",  title: "See whether the lamp is on", risk: "low" },
    { id: "lamp.write", title: "Turn the lamp on and off",   risk: "medium" }
  ],
  // One port serves both the page and the WebSocket the page connects over.
  lan: { enabled: true, bind: "all", httpHandler: serveClient },
  pairing: {
    approve: async (req) => {
      console.log(`\n  "${req.deviceName}" wants: ${req.requestedCaps.join(", ")}`);
      console.log(`  Confirm these digits match the phone: ${req.sas}\n`);
      return true; // replace with a real prompt before shipping
    }
  }
});

server.expose("lamp.status", () => ({ on }), { capability: "lamp.read" });
server.expose("lamp.set", ({ on: next }) => {
  on = Boolean(next);
  server.emit("lamp.changed", { on });
  return { on };
}, { capability: "lamp.write" });

server.declareEvent("lamp.changed", { capability: "lamp.read" });

async function serveClient(req, res) {
  const url = new URL(req.url ?? "/", "http://local.invalid");
  if (url.pathname === "/bundle.js") {
    res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/javascript; charset=utf-8" });
    res.end(await readFile(new URL("./public/bundle.js", import.meta.url)));
    return;
  }
  res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/html; charset=utf-8" });
  res.end(await readFile(new URL("./public/index.html", import.meta.url)));
}

await server.start();
const info = await server.getPairingCode();
console.log(`Pair with: ${info.uri}`);
for (const e of server.connectionEndpoints()) console.log(`  ${e.kind}  ${e.url}`);
```

<Note>
`bind: "all"` is what makes the listener reachable from another device on the
network. `bind: "loopback"` is the safe default for a host that has not decided
yet — it produces no `lan` endpoint at all, because `ws://127.0.0.1` on a phone
means the phone itself.
</Note>

## 4. The client page

`public/client.js`:

```js
import { createSecureCrosslinkClient } from "@crosslink/sdk-browser";

const client = await createSecureCrosslinkClient({
  deviceName: navigator.userAgent.includes("iPhone") ? "iPhone" : "Phone",
  onConfirmPairing: async ({ sas }) =>
    confirm(`Do these digits match the host?\n\n${sas}`)
});

// The host's QR points here with the pairing manifest in the fragment.
const pairUri = new URLSearchParams(location.hash.slice(1)).get("pair");
if (pairUri && !client.listApps().length) {
  await client.pairFromQr(pairUri, ["lamp.read", "lamp.write"]);
  history.replaceState(null, "", location.pathname); // do not leave a used code in history
}

const rpc = await client.connect();

client.onStateChange((state) => {
  document.body.dataset.state = state;
});

const render = ({ on }) => {
  document.querySelector("#lamp").textContent = on ? "ON" : "OFF";
};

render(await rpc.call("lamp.status"));
rpc.subscribe("lamp.changed", render);

document.querySelector("#toggle").onclick = async () => {
  const { on } = await rpc.call("lamp.status");
  await rpc.call("lamp.set", { on: !on });
};
```

Bundle it into the file the host serves:

```bash
npx esbuild public/client.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=public/bundle.js
```

`public/index.html` needs nothing more than a container and
`<script type="module" src="/bundle.js"></script>`.

## 5. Run it

```bash
node host.mjs
```

Open the printed `lan` URL on a phone on the same Wi-Fi, or render `info.qrSvg`
on a screen and scan it. The phone confirms the SAS digits, pairs, and the
toggle works.

## Serving the client from the host

The single-port arrangement above is deliberate, and worth keeping even as the
app grows:

- **One mapping.** Remote access forwards exactly one port. A page on port 3000
  and a socket on port 54676 needs two, and the second one is the one people
  forget.
- **One origin.** The browser stores the page's origin as the app's identity.
  When the page and the socket share it, an installed PWA keeps working without
  cross-origin exceptions.
- **No route mismatch.** A page that loads cannot then fail to reach the socket,
  because they are the same listener.

If your UI is served by a dev server during development (Vite, for example),
add its origin to `lan.allowedOrigins` rather than moving the socket.

## Making it installable

Set `application.pwaConfig` (as above), serve a web app manifest and an icon
from your `httpHandler`, and the phone can add the page to its home screen. The
installed app opens straight into a paired, connected session.

iOS needs one extra thing: a `crosslink://` URI has no handler in the camera
app, so the QR must be an `https://` link to a page. Set
`pairing.bootstrapUrl` to a static HTTPS page you control and
`getPairingCode()` returns a `bootstrapUri` (and a QR for it) instead. Details
in [PWA](/client/pwa).
